5334               	;
5335               	; 	' ======================================================================
5336               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5337               	; 	' ======================================================================
5338               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5339               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5340               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5341               	; 	' of running.
5342               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5343               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5344               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5345               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5346               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5347               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5348               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5349               	; 	'
5350               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5351               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5352               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5353               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5354               	; 	'
5355               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5356               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5357               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5358               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5359               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5360               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5361               	; 	'
5362               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5363               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5364               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5365               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5366               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5367               	; 	'
5368               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5369               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5370               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5371               	; draw_screen:
5372               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5446               	; 		#if NES
5447               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5448               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5449               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5450               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5451               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5452               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5453               	; 		'
5454               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5455               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5456               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5457               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5458               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5459               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5460               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5461               	; 		'
5462               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5463               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.
5464               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,3,32
5465               	; 		WAIT
5466               	; 		#dsrc = #dsrc + 96
5467               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96

5469               	; 		WAIT

5525               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5526               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5527               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5528               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5529               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5530               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5531               	; 	'
5532               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5533               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5534               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5535               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5536               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5537               	; 	'
5538               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5539               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5540               	; 	' above it at all.
5541               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5542               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5543               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5544               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5545               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's

6173               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
6174               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
6175               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
6176               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
6177               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
6178               	; 			'
6179               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
6180               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
6181               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
6182               	; 			'
6183               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
6184               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
6185               	; 			'
6186               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
6187               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
6188               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
6189               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
6190               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
6191               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
6192               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
6193               	; 			' reported from play.
6194               	; 			'
6195               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
6196               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
6197               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
6198               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
6199               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
6200               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
6201               	; 			'
6202               	; 			' HAZGAP is that distance with margin, and it agrees with
6203               	; 			' the original to within 4 px (see the CONST). The pairing
6204               	; 			' is now a fact about the jump rather than an accident of
6205               	; 			' two bytes. assets/checkspace.py measures it and fails the
6206               	; 			' build.
6207               	; 			' THE SECOND SLOT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST, not from its
6208               	; 			' own table byte. Adding HAZGAP to its own `lx AND 63` would
6209               	; 			' still leave the GAP varying by up to 63 px between screens
6210               	; 			' -- the same fault in a politer form, and the reason the two
6211               	; 			' sides of the elevator differed in the first place. Holding
6212               	; 			' slot 0's stagger and adding to that makes the gap exactly
6213               	; 			' HAZGAP on every screen, while slot 0 still lands wherever
6214               	; 			' the table puts it, so the placement variety is untouched.
6215               	; 			' DERIVED FROM THE BAND, not stored. The table used to carry

6316               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6317               	; 			'
6318               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6319               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6320               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6321               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6322               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6323               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6324               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6325               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6326               	; 			'
6327               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6328               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6329               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6330               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6331               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6332               	; 			'
6333               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6334               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6335               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6336               	; 			'
6337               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6338               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6339               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6340               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6341               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6342               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.

7267               cv246
7268               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7269               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7270               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7271               	; 		'
7272               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7273               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7274               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7275               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7276               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
7277               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
7278               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7279               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7280               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
7281               	; 		'
7282               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on

8745               	;
8746               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8747               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8748               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8749               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8750               	; 	'
8751               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8752               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8753               	; 	'
8754               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8755               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8756               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8757               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8758               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8759               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8760               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8761               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8762               	; 	' merged object.
8763               	; 	'
8764               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8765               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8766               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8767               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8768               	; 	'
8769               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8770               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8771               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8772               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8773               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8774               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8775               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8776               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8777               	; 	'
8778               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8779               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8780               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8781               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8782               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8783               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8784               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8785               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8786               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8787               	; 	'
8788               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8789               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8790               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8791               	; 	#if NES
8792               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8793               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8794               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8795               	; 	'
8796               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8797               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8798               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8799               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8800               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8801               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8802               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8803               	; 	'
8804               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8805               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8806               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8807               	; 	'
8808               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8809               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8810               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8811               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8812               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8813               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8814               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8815               	; 	'
8816               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8817               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8818               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8819               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8820               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8821               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8822               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8823               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8824               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8825               	; 	'
8826               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8827               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8828               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8829               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8830               	; 	'
8831               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8832               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8833               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8834               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8835               	; nes_swp16:
8836               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8837               	; 	'
8838               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8839               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8840               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8841               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8842               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8843               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8844               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8845               	; 	'
8846               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8847               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8848               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8849               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8850               	; 	'
8851               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8852               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8853               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8854               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8855               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8856               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8857               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8858               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8859               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8860               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
8861               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
8862               	; 	ntab = 0
8863               	; 	#ncol = 0
8864               	; 	nink = 1
8865               	; 	ncnt = 4
8866               	; 	WAIT
8867               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8868               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
8869               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8870               	; 	WAIT
8871               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8872               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
8873               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8874               	; 	WAIT
8875               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8876               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
8877               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8878               	; 	WAIT
8879               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8880               	; 	RETURN
8881               	;
8882               	; nes_def_raw:
8883               	; 	' Setup only, just like nes_def; never called from the play loop.
8884               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrraw
8885               	; 	RETURN
8886               	;
8887               	; nes_def:
8888               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8889               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8890               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8891               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8892               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8893               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8894               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8895               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8896               	; 	RETURN
8897               	;
8898               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8899               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8900               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8901               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8902               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
8903               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
8904               	; 	'
8905               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
8906               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
8907               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
8908               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
8909               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
8910               	; 	' flashing title screen.
8911               	; 	'
8912               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
8913               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
8914               	; nes_escd:
8915               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
8916               	; 	RETURN
8917               	;

8927               	; 	RETURN
8928               	; 	#endif

9034               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9035               	; 	'

9720               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
9721               	; 	'

9723               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9724               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9725               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9726               	; 	'
9727               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9728               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9729               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9730               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9731               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to

9977               	;
9978               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
9979               	; 	'
9980               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
9981               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
9982               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
9983               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
9984               	; 	'
9985               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
9986               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
9987               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
9988               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9989               	; 	'
9990               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
9991               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
9992               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
9993               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
9994               	; 	'
9995               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
9996               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
9997               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
9998               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
9999               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10000               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10489               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10490               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10491               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10492               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10493               	; 	' runs every pass.
10494               	; 	'
10495               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10496               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10497               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10498               	; 	'
10499               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10500               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10501               	; 	'
10502               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10503               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10504               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10505               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10506               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10507               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10508               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10509               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10510               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10511               	; 	'
10512               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10513               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10514               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10515               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10516               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10517               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no

10619               	;
10620               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10621               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10622               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10623               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10624               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10625               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10626               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10627               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10628               	; 	'
10629               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10630               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10631               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10632               	; 	'
10633               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10634               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10635               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10636               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10637               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10638               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10639               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10640               	; 	'
10641               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10642               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10643               	; 	'
10644               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10645               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10646               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10647               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10648               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10649               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10650               	; 	'
10651               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10652               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10653               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10654               	; 	' before any of this.
10655               	; 	'
10656               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10657               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10658               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10659               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10660               	; 	' journey.
10661               	; 	'
10662               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10663               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10664               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.
10665               	; 	pacc = hacc

10694               	; 			' the east wall stops him too -- he does not slide off the

10699               	; 			' constant the escape target uses, so the place he stops
10700               	; 			' and the place he escapes from cannot disagree.
10701               	; 			' MEASURE THE ROOM, THEN STEP -- and never add past the
10702               	; 			' limit, so this is exact for ANY limit up to 255.
10703               	; 			'
10704               	; 			' The obvious `hx = hx + hspd : IF hx > hlim THEN hx = hlim`
10705               	; 			' is a byte or two cheaper and quietly caps XROOF at 245.
10706               	; 			' `pace_step` can emit two pixels a frame over five frames,
10707               	; 			' so hspd reaches 10; at hlim 252 the sum is 262, which in

10709               	; 			' would TELEPORT TO THE WEST WALL on his last stride. Only
10710               	; 			' at a speed nobody has set yet, which is the worst kind.

11125               	;
11126               	; 	' ======================================================================
11127               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11128               	; 	' ======================================================================
11129               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11130               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11131               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11132               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11133               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11134               	; 	'
11135               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11136               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11137               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11138               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11139               	; 	' broken.
11140               	; 	'
11141               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11142               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11143               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11144               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11145               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11146               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11147               	; 	'
11148               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11149               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11150               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11151               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11152               	; coll_obst:
11153               cvb_COLL_OBST

11519               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11520               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11521               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11522               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11523               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11524               	; 	' away from.
11525               	; 	'
11526               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11527               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11528               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11529               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11530               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11531               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11532               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11533               	; 	'
11534               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11535               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11536               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11537               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11538               	; 	'
11539               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
11540               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.

11543               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once

11708               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11709               	; 	'
11710               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11711               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11712               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11713               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11714               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11715               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11716               	; 	'
11717               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11718               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11719               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11720               	; 	'
11721               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11722               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11723               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11724               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11725               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11726               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11727               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

12413               	; 	' HE IS STRIPED FROM CAP TO HEM. Both stripe colours run the whole upper
12414               	; 	' half, so both boxes span rows 0-15 and neither can be tucked away --
12415               	; 	' affordable only because Kelly's hat moved into a box of its own. His
12416               	; 	' FACE is pushed DOWN instead (hy+3, box 3..18) so it clears the cap
12417               	; 	' rows, where his two stripe boxes plus Kelly's hat and face already
12418               	; 	' make four. Worst line of a meeting: exactly four, nothing dropped.
12419               	; 	' HE RISES A PIXEL ON THE RECOVERY BEATS. A runner is highest at mid-flight
12420               	; 	' and lowest at contact; with the body pinned at a constant y, alternating
12421               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12422               	; 	'
12423               	; 	' One pixel is enough at this size, and it lifts the BODY ONLY -- the legs
12424               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12425               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12426               	; 	' a jump.
12427               	; 	'
12428               	; 	' Beats 2 and 4 are the recoveries, which is exactly `hanim AND 8` -- the
12429               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12430               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12431               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.
12432               	; 	'
12433               	; 	' Safe because HARRY'S COLLISION HAS NO VERTICAL COMPONENT: he is caught on
12434               	; 	' `same level AND |dx| < CATCHR`. Doing this to Kelly would desynchronise
12435               	; 	' his sprite from the ball and biplane windows in DESIGN.md 5a, which is
12436               	; 	' why it is not done to him.
12437               	; 	' THE WHOLE FIGURE RISES, legs included, rather than the body stretching
12438               	; 	' away from the feet. Two reasons, and the second was not the first plan:
12439               	; 	'
12440               	; 	'   * It is what a run does. Mid-flight BOTH feet are off the ground, so
12441               	; 	'     lifting the legs with the body is the correct pose, not a compromise.
12442               	; 	'   * Lifting the body alone opens a one-pixel gap at the waist, and the
12443               	; 	'     torso's bottom row and the legs' top row do not align across it --
12444               	; 	'     green shows through and he reads as coming apart.
12445               	; 	'
12446               	; 	' It also keeps `hfy = hy - 7` and `hy2 = hy + 16` LITERAL, which is not a
12447               	; 	' cosmetic concern: assets/checkbands.py reads each band's draw offset by
12448               	; 	' parsing those exact expressions. Bobbing a differently-named variable
12449               	; 	' made them unreadable and the gate failed the build -- correctly. A
12450               	; 	' checker that can no longer see what it checks has to fail, not shrug.
12451               	; 	' THE RECOVERY LIFT IS A RUNNING THING. Standing on a step he would
12452               	; 	' bob a pixel against a staircase that is itself moving, which reads as

12906               	; 	' ======================================================================
12907               	; 	' THE SCANNER
12908               	; 	' ======================================================================
12909               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
12910               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
12911               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
12912               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
12913               	; 	'
12914               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
12915               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
12916               	; 	'
12917               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
12918               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
12919               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
12920               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
12921               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
12922               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
12923               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
12924               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
12925               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
12926               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
12927               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
12928               	; esc_tick:
12929               cvb_ESC_TICK

12931               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame

12933               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).

12953               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12954               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12955               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12956               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12957               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12958               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12959               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12960               	; 	'
12961               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
12962               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12963               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12964               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12965               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12966               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12967               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

12981               	; 	#if NES
12982               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
12983               	; 	'
12984               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
12985               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
12986               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
12987               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
12988               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
12989               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
12990               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
12991               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
12992               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
12993               	; 	'
12994               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
12995               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
12996               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
12997               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
12998               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
12999               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13000               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13001               	; 	'
13002               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13003               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13004               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13005               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13006               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13007               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13008               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13009               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13010               	; 	' with room to spare.
13011               	; 	'
13012               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13013               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13014               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13015               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13016               	; 	WAIT
13017               	; 	#endif
13018               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13019               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13020               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13021               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13022               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13023               	; 	'
13024               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13025               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13026               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13027               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13028               	; 	'
13029               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13030               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13031               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13032               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13033               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13034               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13035               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13036               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13037               	; 	'
13038               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13039               	; 	' move at all.

13187               	; 	' THREE CHAR ROWS, on 21-23, of which the middle sixteen pixel rows
13188               	; 	' carry the instrument and the outer eight are margin -- four above and
13189               	; 	' four below. The canvas has to be three rows because the four levels
13190               	; 	' need four pixel rows each and 16 px does not fit in two; the margin is

13192               	; 	' stops the radar touching the shop floor above and the screen edge

13367               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13368               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is

13370               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say

13372               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13373               	; 	'
13374               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13375               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13376               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13377               	; 	'
13378               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13379               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13380               	; 	'   +2  GREY

13384               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13385               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13386               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13387               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row

13669               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did

13839               	;
13840               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13841               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13842               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13843               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13844               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13845               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13846               	; scan_wipe:
13847               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13848               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13849               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13850               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13851               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13852               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13853               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13854               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13855               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13856               	; 	'
13857               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13858               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13859               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13860               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13861               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13862               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13863               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13864               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13865               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13866               	; 	'
13867               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13868               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13869               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13870               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13871               	; 	'
13872               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13873               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13874               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns
13875 E906 0200  20 	li r0,5760
     E908 1680     
13876 E90A C800  38 	mov r0,@cvb__SWA
     E90C 20E6     
13877               	; 	#if NES
13878               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
13879               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
13880               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a
13881               	; 	' second hand-kept copy of the same number is exactly the fault recorded
13882               	; 	' in the comment above this routine.
13883               	; 	#swa = #swa + #swa
13884               	; 	#swa = #swa - 4096
13885               	; 	#endif
13886               	; 	' THE SHADOW TAKES ITS BASE FROM THE LINE ABOVE, never from a second
13887               	; 	' copy of the number. renumber.py rewrites that literal out of
13888               	; 	' genart.SCAN_FIRST, and a hand-kept duplicate of it is precisely the
13889               	; 	' fault recorded in the comment above -- one copy moved, the other did
13890               	; 	' not, and the wipe spent months clearing the wrong forty-eight
13891               	; 	' characters. 6 x 64 is 384, which is the size of nsc.
13892               	; 	#if NES
13893               	; 	#nsb = #swa
13894               	; 	#nsi = 0
13895               	; 	#endif
13896               	; 	#if NES
13897               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
13898               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
13899               	; 	' half of what it holds is plane 1; black flights use it too.
13900               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
13901               	; 	'
13902               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
13903               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
13904               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
13905               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
13906               	; 	'
13907               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
13908               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
13909               	; 	' plane 0 and SET plane 1 to reach index 2 (black); see scan_or1.
13910               	; 	' Writing zeros here instead would give the canvas the grey backdrop.
13911               	; 	'
13912               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
13913               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
13914               	; 	' The full 24-row canvas is green; grey margins are separate cells.
13915               	; 	' Plane 0 carries green, plane 1 black, and both together gold.
13916               	; 	FOR swj = 0 TO 11
13917               	; 		FOR swi = 0 TO 63
13918               	; 			swv = #nsi AND 15		' 0-7 plane 0, 8-15 plane 1
13919               	; 			swr = #nsi AND 7		' pixel row inside the tile
13920               	; 			swc = #nsi / 256		' which character row, 0-2
13921               	; 			' NO MARGIN INSIDE THE CANVAS. All twenty-four pixel
13922               	; 			' rows are instrument now -- four bands of six -- and
13923               	; 			' the space around it is the grey strip drawn either
13924               	; 			' side in scan_canvas, which reaches the bottom of the
13925               	; 			' screen. See scan_base.
13926               	; 			swm = 0
13927               	; 			IF swm = 1 THEN
13928               	; 				' grey: shared index 0, both planes clear
13929               	; 				swv = 0
13930               	; 			ELSE
13931               	; 				' green: plane 0 set, plane 1 clear
13932               	; 				IF swv > 7 THEN
13933               	; 					swv = 0
13934               	; 				ELSE
13935               	; 					swv = 255
13936               	; 				END IF

14012               	;
14013               	; 	' THE TWO ACTORS ARE SPRITES; EVERYTHING ELSE IS CHARACTERS.
14014               	; 	'
14015               	; 	' That split is what makes the instrument simple. The floor lines, the
14016               	; 	' flights and the lift car do not move relative to the canvas, so they
14017               	; 	' are pixels in the scanner's own characters and cost nothing to keep.
14018               	; 	' The Kop and the crook DO move, and as sprites they need no colour
14019               	; 	' table, no erase and no priority arithmetic -- they draw over the
14020               	; 	' furniture because sprites always do, and nothing shifts to make room.
14021               	; 	'
14022               	; 	' IT ALSO REMOVED THE BLINK. Kelly flashed because a pixel row of this
14023               	; 	' canvas can only carry one colour, so at close range the two markers
14024               	; 	' merged and the blink was the only thing left to tell them apart. Two
14025               	; 	' sprites are two colours wherever they stand.
14026               	; 	'
14027               	; 	' The furniture is drawn ONCE, by scan_furn. It used to be redrawn every
14028               	; 	' tick because erasing a character-based marker ANDed bits out of
14029               	; 	' whatever it was standing on; there is nothing left to rub it away. The
14030               	; 	' car still redraws itself, because the car actually moves.
14031               	; 	' -- the lift car. IT WAS FLICKERING, and the cause was not the drawing
14032               	; 	' but the ERASING: scan_elev cleared its three cells and put them back
14033               	; 	' every tick, whether or not the car had moved, so several times a second
14034               	; 	' there was a window with the pixels off. A sprite has no erase at all --

14036               	; 	' two markers, so the Kop and the crook pass over it without either of

14972               	; 	' read as intermittent corruption.

14977               	; 	' queued, and a WAIT per run made its twelve runs appear one frame at a

15041               	;
15042               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15043               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15044               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15045               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15046               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15047               	; 	'
15048               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15049               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15050               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15051               	; 	'
15052               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15053               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15054               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15055               	; 	'
15056               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15057               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15058               	; 	'
15059               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15060               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15061               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15062               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15063               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15064               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15065               	; 	'
15066               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15067               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15068               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15069               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15070               	; 	'
15071               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15072               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15073               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15074               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15075               	; bonus_count:
15076               cvb_BONUS_COUNT
15077               	; 	' THE CLOCK IS ABOUT TO BE COUNTED DOWN, so the field has to be up --
15078               	; 	' the round can end on any phase of the low-time flash, and a tally
15079               	; 	' running into a blanked field would draw nothing at all.
15080               	; 	GOSUB time_show
15081 EEE6 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     EEE8 A980     
15082 EEEA EE42     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15083               	; 	#bval = 10

15195               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15196               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15197               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15198               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15199               	; 	'
15200               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15201               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15202               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15203               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15204               	; 	' counting stops.

15207               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15208               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15209               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15210               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15211               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15212               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15213               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.

15439               	;
15440               	; 	' Silence every channel FIRST. SOUND latches, and the per-channel decay
15441               	; 	' counters are not ticked inside this loop -- a tone still sounding when
15442               	; 	' the pause starts would hang for its whole duration, which is the classic
15443               	; 	' CVBasic sticky-audio failure.
15444               	; 	' EVERY CHANNEL OFF, AND THE DECAY COUNTERS WITH THEM. The counters are
15445               	; 	' ticked by the main loop, so anything still sounding when the loop stops
15446               	; 	' -- for a capture, a death, the bonus count -- sustains for as long as
15447               	; 	' whatever replaced the loop takes. That is where the long beep over the
15448               	; 	' bonus tally came from: not the tally's own note, which turns itself off
15449               	; 	' after every unit, but a footstep or a hit that was still ringing when
15450               	; 	' Harry was caught.
15451               	; snd_off:
15452               cvb_SND_OFF
15453               	; 	' EVERY CHANNEL sfx_tick CAN WRITE, AND CHANNEL 3 IS ONE OF THEM. This
15454               	; 	' routine was written when the footstep was a pair of tones on channel 0
15455               	; 	' and it still named only 0, 1 and 2 after the footstep moved to the

15570               	;
15571               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15572               	; 	'
15573               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15574               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15575               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15576               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15577               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15578               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15579               	; 	'
15580               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15581               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15582               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15583               	; 	'
15584               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15585               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15586               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15587               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15588               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15589               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15590               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15591               	; 	'
15592               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15593               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15594               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15595               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15596               	; 	'
15597               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15598               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15599               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15600               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15601               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15602               	; 	'
15603               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15604               	; 	' did not finish.
15605               	; pause_beat:
15606               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
15607               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
15608 F150 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F152 A980

15613               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15614               	; 	'
15615               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

15617               	; 	' decay counters are in frames and every effect would ring twice as long.

16031               	;
16032               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16033               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16034               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16035               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16036               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16037               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16038               	;
16039               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16040               	; 	'
16041               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16042               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16043               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16044               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16045               	; 	'
16046               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16047               	; 	'
16048               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16049               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16050               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16051               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16052               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16053               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16054               	; 	'
16055               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16056               	; 	'
16057               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16058               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16059               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16060               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16061               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16062               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16063               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16064               	; 	'
16065               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16066               	; 	'
16067               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16068               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16069               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16070               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16071               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16072               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16073               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16074               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16075               	; 	'
16076               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16077               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16078               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16079               	; 	'
16080               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16081               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16082               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16083               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16084               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16085               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16086               	; 	'
16087               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16088               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.

16090               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block

16093               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of

16303 F57E 0450  20 	b *r0
16304               	;
16305               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16306               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16307               	; 	'
16308               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16309               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16310               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16311               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16312               	; 	'
16313               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16314               	; 	'
16315               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16316               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16317               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16318               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16319               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16320               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16321               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16322               	; 	'
16323               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16324               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16325               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16326               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16327               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16328               	; 	'
16329               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16330               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16331               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16332               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16333               	; 	#if TI994A
16334               	; 	BANK 2
16335      0A7E     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept
